# easy-cast 0.4.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/easy-cast/0.4.1

# Easy-cast

Type conversion, success expected

Use the `Conv` and `Cast` traits when:

- `From`and- `Into`are not enough
- it is expected that the value can be represented exactly by the target type
- you could use `as`, but want some assurance it's doing the right thing
- you are converting numbers (future versions *might*consider supporting other conversions)

Use the `ConvFloat` and `CastFloat` traits when:

- You are converting from `f32`or`f64`
- You specifically want the nearest or ceiling or floor, but don't need detailed control over rounding (e.g. round-to-even)

## Assertions

All type conversions which are potentially fallible assert on failure in debug builds. In release builds assertions may be omitted, thus making incorrect conversions possible.

If the `always_assert` feature flag is set, assertions will be turned on in
all builds. Some additional feature flags are available for finer-grained
control (see [Cargo.toml](https://docs.rs/Cargo.toml)).

## MSRV and no_std

The Minumum Supported Rust Version is 1.32.0 (first release of Edition 2018).

By default, `std` support is required. With default features disabled `no_std`
is supported, but the `ConvFloat` and `CastFloat` traits are unavailable.
Enabling the `libm` feature will re-enable these traits.

## Copyright and Licence

optionally add themselves to this list.

## Expand description

Type conversion, success expected

This library exists to make fallible numeric type conversions easy, without
resorting to the `as` keyword.

- `Conv`- `From`
- `Cast`- `Conv`- `Into`- `From`
- `ConvApprox`- `CastApprox`
- `ConvFloat`- `CastFloat`

If you are wondering “why not just use `as`”, there are a few reasons:

- integer conversions may silently truncate or sign-extend which does not preserve value
- prior to Rust 1.45.0 float-to-int conversions were not fully defined; since this version they use saturating conversion (NaN converts to 0)
- you want some assurance (at least in debug builds) that the conversion will preserve values correctly

Why might you *not* want to use this library?

- You want saturating / truncating / other non-value-preserving conversion
- You want to convert non-numeric types (`From``Conv`
- You want a thoroughly tested library (we’re not quite there yet)

[§](https://docs.rs#error-handling)Error handling

All traits support two methods:

- `try_*`methods return a- `Result`and always fail if the correct conversion is not possible
- other methods may panic or return incorrect results

In debug builds, methods not returning `Result` must panic on failure. As
with the overflow checks on Rust’s standard integer arithmetic, this is
considered a tool for finding logic errors. In release builds, these methods
are permitted to return defined but incorrect results similar to the `as`
keyword.

If the `always_assert` feature flag is set, assertions will be turned on in

then the library supports `no_std`. In this case, [ ConvFloat](https://docs.rs/trait.ConvFloat.html) and

# Conv in easy_cast - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/easy-cast/latest/easy_cast/trait.Conv.html

`pub trait Conv<T>: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [try_conv](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_conv)(v: T) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>;
    // Provided method
    fn [conv](https://docs.rs#method.conv)(v: T) -> Self { ... }
}## Expand description

Like [ From](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html), but supports fallible conversions

This trait is intented to be an extension over [ From](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html), also supporting
fallible conversions of numeric types.
Since Rust does not yet have stable support for handling conflicting
implementations (specialization or otherwise), only conversions between
the most important numeric types are supported for now.

The sister-trait [ Cast](https://docs.rs/trait.Cast.html) supports “into” style usage.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Convert from `T` to `Self`

This method must return the same result as [ Self::try_conv](https://docs.rs/trait.Conv.html#tymethod.try_conv) where that
method succeeds, but differs in the handling of errors:

- In debug builds the method panics on error
- Otherwise, the method may panic or may return a different value,
but like with the `as`keyword all results must be well-defined and*safe*.

Default implementations use [ Self::try_conv](https://docs.rs/trait.Conv.html#tymethod.try_conv) and panic on error.
Implementations provided by this library will panic in debug builds
or if the

`always_assert` feature flag is used, and otherwise will
behave identically to the `as` keyword.This mirrors the behaviour of Rust’s overflow checks on integer arithmetic in that it is a tool for diagnosing logic errors where success is expected.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

## Implementations on Foreign Types[§](https://docs.rs#foreign-impls)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/easy_cast/impl_basic.rs.html#209-241)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Conv%3C(S0,+S1,+S2,+S3,+S4,+S5)%3E-for-(T0,+T1,+T2,+T3,+T4,+T5))### impl<S0, S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, T0, T1, T2, T3, T4, T5> [Conv](https://docs.rs/trait.Conv.html)<[(S0, S1, S2, S3, S4, S5)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)> for [(T0, T1, T2, T3, T4, T5)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/easy_cast/impl_basic.rs.html#209-241)

# Cast in easy_cast - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/easy-cast/latest/easy_cast/trait.Cast.html

## Expand description

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Try converting from `Self` to `T`

Use this method to explicitly handle errors.

Cast from `Self` to `T`

Use this method *only* where success is expected: implementations are
permitted to panic or silently return a different (safe, defined) value
on error.

In debug builds, implementations must panic.

Implementations by this library will panic in debug builds or if the
`always_assert` feature flag is used, otherwise conversions have the
same behaviour as the `as` keyword.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

---

# ConvApprox in easy_cast - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/easy-cast/latest/easy_cast/trait.ConvApprox.html

`pub trait ConvApprox<T>: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [try_conv_approx](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_conv_approx)(x: T) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>;
    // Provided method
    fn [conv_approx](https://docs.rs#method.conv_approx)(x: T) -> Self { ... }
}## Expand description

Like [ From](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html), but for approximate numerical conversions

On success, the result must be approximately the same as the input value:
the difference must be smaller than the precision of the target type.
For example, one may have `i32::conv_approx(1.9f32) = 1` or
`f32::conv_approx(1f64 + (f32::EPSILON as f64) / 2.0) = 1.0`.

Precise rounding mode should usually be truncation (round towards zero),
but this is not required. Use [ ConvFloat](https://docs.rs/trait.ConvFloat.html) where a specific rounding mode
is required.

The sister-trait [ CastApprox](https://docs.rs/trait.CastApprox.html) supports “into” style usage.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/easy_cast/traits.rs.html#116)#### fn [try_conv_approx](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_conv_approx)(x: T) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/easy_cast/traits.rs.html#116)

#### fn [try_conv_approx](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_conv_approx)(x: T) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>

Try converting from `T` to `Self`, allowing approximation of value

This conversion may truncate excess precision not supported by the
target type, so long as the *value* is approximately equal, from the
point of view of precision of the target type.

This method should allow approximate conversion, but fail on input not (approximately) in the target’s range.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/easy_cast/traits.rs.html#137-141)#### fn [conv_approx](https://docs.rs#method.conv_approx)(x: T) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/easy_cast/traits.rs.html#137-141)

#### fn [conv_approx](https://docs.rs#method.conv_approx)(x: T) -> Self

Converting from `T` to `Self`, allowing approximation of value

This method must return the same result as [ Self::try_conv_approx](https://docs.rs/trait.ConvApprox.html#tymethod.try_conv_approx)
where that method succeeds, but differs in the handling of errors:

- In debug builds the method panics on error
- Otherwise, the method may panic or may return a different value,
but like with the `as`keyword all results must be well-defined and*safe*.

Default implementations use [ Self::try_conv_approx](https://docs.rs/trait.ConvApprox.html#tymethod.try_conv_approx) and panic on error.
Implementations provided by this library will panic in debug builds
or if the

`always_assert` feature flag is used, and otherwise will
behave identically to the `as` keyword.This mirrors the behaviour of Rust’s overflow checks on integer arithmetic in that it is a tool for diagnosing logic errors where success is expected.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

---

Like [ Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html), but for

`ConvApprox`On success, the result must be approximately the same as the input value:
the difference must be smaller than the precision of the target type.
For example, one may have `1.9f32.cast_approx() = 1`.

is required.

# ConvFloat in easy_cast - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/easy-cast/latest/easy_cast/trait.ConvFloat.html

`pub trait ConvFloat<T>: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    // Required methods
    fn [try_conv_trunc](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_conv_trunc)(x: T) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>;
[try_conv_nearest](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_conv_nearest)(x: T) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>;
[try_conv_floor](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_conv_floor)(x: T) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>;
[try_conv_ceil](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_conv_ceil)(x: T) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>;
    // Provided methods
    fn [conv_trunc](https://docs.rs#method.conv_trunc)(x: T) -> Self { ... }
[conv_nearest](https://docs.rs#method.conv_nearest)(x: T) -> Self { ... }
[conv_floor](https://docs.rs#method.conv_floor)(x: T) -> Self { ... }
[conv_ceil](https://docs.rs#method.conv_ceil)(x: T) -> Self { ... }
}## Expand description

Nearest / floor / ceiling conversions from floating point types

This trait is explicitly for conversions from floating-point values to integers, supporting four rounding modes.

As with [ Conv](https://docs.rs/trait.Conv.html), the

`try_conv_*` methods must be implemented and must fail
if conversion to the expected value is not possible. If the source is non-
finite (`inf` or `NaN`), then `Error::Range` should be returned.The `conv_*` methods each have a default implementation over the `try_..`
variant which panics on failure. Implementations handle errors as follows:

- In debug builds, the methods must panic
- Otherwise, the method may panic or may return a different value; all
results must be well-defined and *safe*.
- Implementations provided by this library will also panic if the
`always_assert`or`assert_float`feature flag is used.

The sister-trait [ CastFloat](https://docs.rs/trait.CastFloat.html) supports “into” style usage.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/easy_cast/traits.rs.html#223)

Rounds towards zero (same as `as`).

Try converting to the nearest integer

Half-way cases are rounded away from `0`.

# CastFloat in easy_cast - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/easy-cast/latest/easy_cast/trait.CastFloat.html

```
pub trait CastFloat<T> {
    // Required methods
    fn
```
[cast_trunc](https://docs.rs#tymethod.cast_trunc)(self) -> T;
[cast_nearest](https://docs.rs#tymethod.cast_nearest)(self) -> T;
[cast_floor](https://docs.rs#tymethod.cast_floor)(self) -> T;
[cast_ceil](https://docs.rs#tymethod.cast_ceil)(self) -> T;
[try_cast_trunc](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_cast_trunc)(self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<T>;
[try_cast_nearest](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_cast_nearest)(self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<T>;
[try_cast_floor](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_cast_floor)(self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<T>;
[try_cast_ceil](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_cast_ceil)(self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<T>;
}## Expand description

Use:

-
`try_cast_*`methods to explicitly handle errors
-
`cast_*`methods*only*where success is expected. Implementations are permitted to panic or silently return a different (safe, defined) value on error.In debug builds, implementations must panic. Implementations by this library will panic in debug builds or if the `always_assert`or`assert_float`feature flag is used, otherwise conversions have similar behaviour to the`as`keyword.

This trait is automatically implemented for every implementation of
[ ConvFloat](https://docs.rs/trait.ConvFloat.html).

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/easy_cast/traits.rs.html#294)#### fn [cast_floor](https://docs.rs#tymethod.cast_floor)(self) -> T

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/easy_cast/traits.rs.html#294)

#### fn [cast_floor](https://docs.rs#tymethod.cast_floor)(self) -> T

Cast the floor to an integer

Returns the largest integer less than or equal to `self`.

Cast the ceiling to an integer

Returns the smallest integer greater than or equal to `self`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/easy_cast/traits.rs.html#303)#### fn [try_cast_trunc](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_cast_trunc)(self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<T>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/easy_cast/traits.rs.html#303)

#### fn [try_cast_trunc](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_cast_trunc)(self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<T>

Try converting to integer with truncation

Rounds towards zero (same as `as`).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/easy_cast/traits.rs.html#307)#### fn [try_cast_nearest](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_cast_nearest)(self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<T>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/easy_cast/traits.rs.html#307)

#### fn [try_cast_nearest](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_cast_nearest)(self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<T>

Try converting to the nearest integer

Half-way cases are rounded away from `0`.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# easy-cast 0.5.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/easy-cast/latest/source/CHANGELOG.md

Changelog
=========
##[0.5.4] — 2025-11-20-Bump MSRV to 1.79.0
- Support `Conv`, `Cast` for `core::ops::Range` and other range types (#38)
- Support `Conv`, `Cast` for `core::num::{Saturating, Wrapping}` (#38)
- Support `Conv`, `Cast` for `core::num::NonZero` (#39)
##[0.5.3] — 2024-12-12-Bump MSRV to 1.60.0 and use Edition 2021 (#30)
##[0.5.2] — 2022-12-22-Support cast to self, useful in generics (#28)
##[0.5.1] — 2022-10-14-Document feature assert_digits and imply by always_assert (#26)
##[0.5.0] — 2022-08-19-Reorganise code (#20)
- Bump MSRV to 1.53.0 (#21)
- Add default implementations of `conv` methods over equivalent `try_conv`variant to facilitate custom implementations (#21)
- Add `ConvApprox` and `CastApprox`, supporting approximate conversions
with unspecified rounding, implemented for `f64 → f32` and all type
conversions supported by `Conv` (#21)
- Support `Conv` and `ConvFloat` for arrays and tuples (#21)
- Remove `impl<T> Conv<T> for T` (#21)
- Add `easy_cast::Result` type alias (#22)
- Move traits into new `easy_cast::traits` public module (#23)
##[0.4.4] — 2021-04-12-Fix negative int to float digits check (#18)
##[0.4.3] — 2021-04-12-Unify some macros via `impl_int_generic` (#16)
- Improve error messages in asserts (#17)
##[0.4.2] — 2021-04-03-Fix `i16::conv(1usize)` (#15)
- Update README (#15)
##[0.4.1] — 2021-04-01-Fix `conv(0)` from int to float (#14)
##[0.4.0] — 2021-04-01-Add `try_conv` and `try_cast` methods (#12)
- Add `try_conv_nearest` etc. (#12)
- Removed `Conv<f64> for f32` (#12)
- Replaced `assert_range` and `assert_non_neg` with `assert_int` (#12)
- MSRV is 1.32.0 (#12)
##[0.3.0] — 2021-03-29-Add `conv_trunc` / `cast_trunc` (#11)
- Explicitly support Rust 1.36.0 (and potentially older; #10)
- Support `no_std` (#10)
- Fix rounding for `floor` on negative values (#10)
##[0.2.0] — 2021-03-20-Add feature flags controlling assert behaviour
- Remove restrictions on isize/usize (#6)
- Fix bad revert checks (#6)

---

# easy-cast 0.5.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/easy-cast/latest/source/README.md

```
Easy-cast
=========
[![Test Status](https://github.com/kas-gui/easy-cast/workflows/Tests/badge.svg?event=push)](https://github.com/kas-gui/easy-cast/actions)
[![Docs](https://docs.rs/easy-cast/badge.svg)](https://docs.rs/easy-cast)
Type conversion, success expected
This library exists to make fallible numeric type conversions easy, without
resorting to the `as` keyword.
-   ---
If you are wondering "why not just use `as`", there are a few reasons:
-   --
Why might you *not* want to use this library?
-   --
All traits support two methods:
-   -
In debug builds, methods not returning `Result` must panic on failure. As
with the overflow checks on Rust's standard integer arithmetic, this is
considered a tool for finding logic errors. In release builds, these methods
are permitted to return defined but incorrect results similar to the `as`
keyword.
If the `always_assert` feature flag is set, assertions will be turned on in
all builds. Some additional feature flags are available for finer-grained
control (see `Cargo.toml`).
Performance is "good enough that it hasn't been a concern".
In debug builds and when `always_assert` is enabled, the priority is testing
but overhead should be small.
In release builds without `always_assert`, `conv*` methods should reduce to
`x as T` (with necessary additions for rounding).
When the crate's default features are disabled (and `std` is not enabled)
then the library supports `no_std`. In this case, [`ConvFloat`] and
[`CastFloat`] are only available if the `libm` optional dependency is
enabled.
The Minumum Supported Rust Version is 1.79.0 (`IntoIterator for [T; N]`).
By default, `std` support is required. With default features disabled `no_std`
is supported, but the `ConvFloat` and `CastFloat` traits are unavailable.
Enabling the `libm` feature will re-enable these traits.
Copyright and Licence
The [COPYRIGHT](COPYRIGHT) file includes a list of contributors who claim
copyright on this project. This list may be incomplete; new contributors may
optionally add themselves to this list.
The easy-cast library is published under the terms of the Apache License, Version 2.0.
You may obtain a copy of this licence from the [LICENSE](LICENSE) file or on
the following webpage: <https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0>
```

# libm 0.2.16 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/libm/0.2.16

`libm`

A Rust implementations of the C math library.

## Usage

`libm` provides fallback implementations for Rust's [float math functions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.f32.html) in
`core`, and the [ core_float_math](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/137578) feature. If what is available suits your
needs, there is no need to add

`libm` as a dependency.If more functionality is needed, this crate can also be used directly:

```
[]
 = "0.2.11"
```
## Contributing

Please check [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://docs.rs/CONTRIBUTING.md)

## Minimum Rust version policy

This crate supports rustc 1.63 and newer.

## License

Usage is under the MIT license, available at
[https://opensource.org/license/mit](https://opensource.org/license/mit).

### Contribution

Contributions are licensed under both the MIT license and the Apache License,
Version 2.0, available at [https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0). Unless
you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for
inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be
dual licensed as mentioned, without any additional terms or conditions.

See [LICENSE.txt](https://docs.rs/LICENSE.txt) for full details.

# no_panic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/no-panic/^0.1.35/

## Expand description

A Rust attribute macro to require that the compiler prove a function can’t ever panic.

```
[dependencies]
no-panic = "0.1"
```
```
use no_panic::no_panic;
#[no_panic]
fn demo(s: &str) -> &str {
    &s[1..]
}
fn main() {
    println!("{}", demo("input string"));
}
```
If the function does panic (or the compiler fails to prove that the function cannot panic), the program fails to compile with a linker error that identifies the function name. Let’s trigger that by passing a string that cannot be sliced at the first byte:

```
   Compiling no-panic-demo v0.0.1
error: linking with `cc` failed: exit code: 1
  |
  = note: /no-panic-demo/target/release/deps/no_panic_demo-7170785b672ae322.no_p
anic_demo1-cba7f4b666ccdbcbbf02b7348e5df1b2.rs.rcgu.o: In function `_$LT$no_pani
c_demo..demo..__NoPanic$u20$as$u20$core..ops..drop..Drop$GT$::drop::h72f8f423002
b8d9f':
          no_panic_demo1-cba7f4b666ccdbcbbf02b7348e5df1b2.rs:(.text._ZN72_$LT$no
_panic_demo..demo..__NoPanic$u20$as$u20$core..ops..drop..Drop$GT$4drop17h72f8f42
3002b8d9fE+0x2): undefined reference to `
          ERROR[no-panic]: detected panic in function `demo`
          '
          collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
```
The error is not stellar but notice the ERROR[no-panic] part at the end that provides the name of the offending function.

[§](https://docs.rs#caveats)Caveats

-
Functions that require some amount of optimization to prove that they do not panic may no longer compile in debug mode after being marked `#[no_panic]`.
-
Panic detection happens at link time across the entire dependency graph, so any Cargo commands that do not invoke a linker will not trigger panic detection. This includes `cargo build`of library crates and`cargo check`of binary and library crates.
-
The attribute is useless in code built with `panic = "abort"`. Code must be built with`panic = "unwind"`(the default) in order for any panics to be detected. After confirming absence of panics, you can of course still ship your software as a`panic = "abort"`build.
-
Const functions are not supported. The attribute will fail to compile if placed on a `const fn`.

If you find that code requires optimization to pass `#[no_panic]`, either
make no-panic an optional dependency that you only enable in release builds,
or add a section like the following to your Cargo.toml or .cargo/config.toml
to enable very basic optimization in debug builds.

```
[profile.dev]
opt-level = 1
```
If the code that you need to prove isn’t panicking makes function calls to non-generic non-inline functions from a different crate, you may need thin LTO enabled for the linker to deduce those do not panic.

```
[profile.release]
lto = "thin"
```
If thin LTO isn’t cutting it, the next thing to try would be fat LTO with a single codegen unit:

```
[profile.release]
lto = "fat"
codegen-units = 1
```
If you want no_panic to just assume that some function you call doesn’t
panic, and get Undefined Behavior if it does at runtime, see
[dtolnay/no-panic#16](https://github.com/dtolnay/no-panic/issues/16); try wrapping that call in an `unsafe extern "C"`
wrapper.

[§](https://docs.rs#acknowledgments)Acknowledgments

The linker error technique is based on [Kixunil](https://github.com/Kixunil)’s crate [ dont_panic](https://github.com/Kixunil/dont_panic).
Check out that crate for other convenient ways to require absence of panics.

# Libm in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/struct.Libm.html

`pub struct Libm<T>(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

Generic helper for libm functions, abstracting over f32 and f64.

[§](https://docs.rs#type-parameter)Type Parameter:

- `T`: Either- `f32`or- `f64`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use libm::{self, Libm};
const PI_F32: f32 = 3.1415927410e+00;
const PI_F64: f64 = 3.1415926535897931160e+00;
assert!(Libm::<f32>::cos(0.0f32) == libm::cosf(0.0));
assert!(Libm::<f32>::sin(PI_F32) == libm::sinf(PI_F32));
assert!(Libm::<f64>::cos(0.0f64) == libm::cos(0.0));
assert!(Libm::<f64>::sin(PI_F64) == libm::sin(PI_F64));
```

# acos in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/fn.acos.html

Computes the inverse cosine (arc cosine) of the input value.
Arguments must be in the range -1 to 1.
Returns values in radians, in the range of 0 to pi.

---

# acosf in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/fn.acosf.html

Computes the inverse cosine (arc cosine) of the input value.
Arguments must be in the range -1 to 1.
Returns values in radians, in the range of 0 to pi.

---

# acosh in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/fn.acosh.html

## Expand description

Inverse hyperbolic cosine (f64)

Calculates the inverse hyperbolic cosine of `x`.
Is defined as `log(x + sqrt(x*x-1))`.
`x` must be a number greater than or equal to 1.

---

# acoshf in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/fn.acoshf.html

## Expand description

Inverse hyperbolic cosine (f32)

Calculates the inverse hyperbolic cosine of `x`.
Is defined as `log(x + sqrt(x*x-1))`.
`x` must be a number greater than or equal to 1.

---

# asin in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/fn.asin.html

Computes the inverse sine (arc sine) of the argument x.
Arguments to asin must be in the range -1 to 1.
Returns values in radians, in the range of -pi/2 to pi/2.

---

# asinf in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/fn.asinf.html

Computes the inverse sine (arc sine) of the argument x.
Arguments to asin must be in the range -1 to 1.
Returns values in radians, in the range of -pi/2 to pi/2.

---

# asinh in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/fn.asinh.html

## Expand description

Inverse hyperbolic sine (f64)

Calculates the inverse hyperbolic sine of `x`.
Is defined as `sgn(x)*log(|x|+sqrt(x*x+1))`.

---

# asinhf in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/fn.asinhf.html

## Expand description

Inverse hyperbolic sine (f32)

Calculates the inverse hyperbolic sine of `x`.
Is defined as `sgn(x)*log(|x|+sqrt(x*x+1))`.

# atan in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/fn.atan.html

## Expand description

Arctangent (f64)

Computes the inverse tangent (arc tangent) of the input value. Returns a value in radians, in the range of -pi/2 to pi/2.

---

# atan2 in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/fn.atan2.html

Computes the inverse tangent (arc tangent) of y/x.
Produces the correct result even for angles near pi/2 or -pi/2 (that is, when x is near 0).
Returns a value in radians, in the range of -pi to pi.

---

# atan2f in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/fn.atan2f.html

Computes the inverse tangent (arc tangent) of y/x.
Produces the correct result even for angles near pi/2 or -pi/2 (that is, when x is near 0).
Returns a value in radians, in the range of -pi to pi.

---

# atanf in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/fn.atanf.html

## Expand description

Arctangent (f32)

Computes the inverse tangent (arc tangent) of the input value. Returns a value in radians, in the range of -pi/2 to pi/2.

# atanh in libm - Rust

# erf in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/fn.erf.html

Calculates an approximation to the “error function”, which estimates
the probability that an observation will fall within x standard
deviations of the mean (assuming a normal distribution).

---

# erfc in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/fn.erfc.html

## Expand description

Complementary error function (f64)

Calculates the complementary probability.
Is `1 - erf(x)`. Is computed directly, so that you can use it to avoid
the loss of precision that would result from subtracting
large probabilities (on large `x`) from 1.

---

# erfcf in libm - Rust

## Expand description

# expm1 in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/fn.expm1.html

## Expand description

Exponential, base *e*, of x-1 (f64)

Calculates the exponential of `x` and subtract 1, that is, *e* raised
to the power `x` minus 1 (where *e* is the base of the natural
system of logarithms, approximately 2.71828).
The result is accurate even for small values of `x`,
where using `exp(x)-1` would lose many significant digits.

---

# expm1f in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/fn.expm1f.html

## Expand description

Exponential, base *e*, of x-1 (f32)

Calculates the exponential of `x` and subtract 1, that is, *e* raised
to the power `x` minus 1 (where *e* is the base of the natural
system of logarithms, approximately 2.71828).
The result is accurate even for small values of `x`,
where using `exp(x)-1` would lose many significant digits.

# fdim in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/fn.fdim.html

## Expand description

Positive difference (f64)

Determines the positive difference between arguments, returning:

- x - y if x > y, or
- +0 if x <= y, or
- NAN if either argument is NAN.

A range error may occur.

# fmax in libm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libm/^0.2.1/fn.fmax.html

## Expand description

Return the greater of two arguments or, if either argument is NaN, the other argument.

This coincides with IEEE 754-2011 `maxNum`. The result disregards signed zero (meaning if
the inputs are -0.0 and +0.0, either may be returned).

---
